summary:
Tilion is a landing-site planner for the lunar south pole. Pick a site and a date, and
Tilion shows what a lander will actually see: the Sun and the Earth moving over the real
skyline, built from NASA LOLA terrain and SPICE DE440 ephemerides.

What no other public tool gives in one place:
- Sunset countdown with an error band: the time to sunset and Earthset, plus how far
  it moves if the terrain is 1 sigma higher or lower.
- Main blocker: names the ridge that steals the Sun, with its distance, height and the
  hours of light it costs. Skyline layers show whether a near ridge or a far massif
  sets the horizon.
- Any point, not only a catalog: click anywhere near the pole and the browser computes
  its horizon from the 240 m terrain map.
- Date slip planner: give a slip range and a radius, and Tilion ranks site × date
  alternatives with a 0–100 score and a rover route over the terrain.
- Mission engineering: smallest battery to survive the dark, Earth elevation margin,
  DSN station in view, Earth eclipses, ground temperature, a one-page mission brief.
- Proof built in: a NASA check screen compares Tilion with JPL Horizons, Apollo landings
  and PGDA 69 maps, and shows the checks that fail.

WHAT IT DOES

Tilion is a landing-site navigator for the lunar south pole. A mission planner picks a site

and a date and sees, on one screen, what a lander will see: the Sun and the Earth moving over

the real terrain skyline. When the landing date slips, Tilion finds the best replacement

site and date nearby. Today this takes manual work across JPL Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek.

KEY FEATURES

- Real skyline, not a flat horizon. A horizon panorama and a 3D view from the site, built

from NASA LOLA terrain, with the Sun as a limb-darkened 0.53° disc and the Earth.

- Sunset countdown with an error band. Time to the next sunset and Earthset, plus how far it

WHAT IT DOES

Tilion is a landing-site navigator for the lunar south pole. A mission planner picks a site

and a date and sees, on one screen, what a lander will see: the Sun and the Earth moving over

the real terrain skyline. When the landing date slips, Tilion finds the best replacement

site and date nearby. Today this takes manual work across JPL Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek.

KEY FEATURES

- Real skyline, not a flat horizon. A horizon panorama and a 3D view from the site, built

from NASA LOLA terrain, with the Sun as a limb-darkened 0.53° disc and the Earth.

- Sunset countdown with an error band. Time to the next sunset and Earthset, plus how far it

moves if the terrain is 1 sigma higher or lower (from the LOLA height error layer).

- Main blocker. Names the ridge that steals the Sun: azimuth, distance, height and the hours

of light it costs. Skyline layers show whether a near ridge or a far massif sets the horizon.

- Any point, not only a catalog. 24 curated sites (Artemis III candidate regions, CLPS

landers, other national missions, Apollo), or click any point from 60°S to 90°S: the

browser computes its horizon from the LOLA 240 m map.

- Communication windows. A dated calendar of Sun and Earth windows with an OK / MARGINAL /

FAIL verdict, Earth elevation margin, and which DSN complex (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra)

sees the site.

- Date slip planner. Give a landing date, slip range, search radius and rover waypoints.

Tilion ranks site × date alternatives by a 0–100 score (power, night survival, comms,

longest blackout, sunset margin) and shows every term. The rover route follows the LOLA

elevation profile. A slip report says in plain sentences what changed. The plan is a

shareable link.

- Mission engineering. Smallest battery to survive the dark, energy with tilted panels,

Earth eclipses, ground temperature, and a one-page mission brief.

- Proof built in. A NASA check screen compares every number with an independent reference

and shows the checks that fail.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline precomputes everything. It builds a horizon mask for each site from LOLA

terrain (20 m within 5 km of a polar site, then 80 m and 240 m) for an observer 2 m above

the surface. It computes hourly Sun and Earth positions with NASA NAIF SPICE (DE440, frame

MOON_ME, light time and aberration, TDB time). The web app reads static files: no server,

no install, one link.

HOW WE VALIDATE

Sun and Earth positions differ from JPL Horizons by at most 1e-06° at a 0.002° tolerance.

The Sun at 8 of 8 Apollo landings is within 0.3°. Earth visibility matches NASA PGDA 69 maps

at 18 of 18 sites within 5 percentage points. On the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge our

illumination is inside the NASA corridor of Barker et al. 2021 at 7 of 7 points. Tolerances

were fixed before each run, and the app shows the failures too.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

One screen replaces several expert tools for a fast "what if the date slips" decision. Near

the pole a flat-Moon model moves sunset by hours to days; real terrain decides power and

communication. Teachers and the public see why a small change of site or date changes

power and contact at the lunar pole.

CREATIVITY

Tilion does not ask for trust; it shows evidence. Every validated number carries its

reference and tolerance, and failed checks stay visible. The uncertainty band, the main

blocker and the skyline layers explain why a site is dark, not only that it is dark.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Open data only. Terrain covers 60–90°S; north of that the Moon is a sphere, marked "no

terrain". Cold-trap areas are candidates, not detected ice. Score weights and the 48 h

sunset margin are our assumptions. Earth + DSN is geometry only, with no antenna schedules.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, MapLibre GL JS, GSAP; Python, spiceypy (NAIF SPICE),

rasterio, NumPy; Vitest, pytest, Playwright; GitHub Actions; Caddy static hosting.


SOURCE CODE

Public repository: https://github.com/IR630/tilion

This is a clean public copy of our code. The full development repository, with commit history, issues and pull requests, is private. If the judges need it, contact us and we will give access.
